clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC34A3, encoding the proximal tubular sodium-phosphate cotransporter NaPi-IIc.
Renal phosphate wasting drives hypophosphataemia and rickets or osteomalacia, with a reduced tubular maximum for phosphate reabsorption relative to filtration.
Unlike the FGF23-driven forms of hypophosphataemic rickets, circulating fibroblast growth factor 23 is low or normal, so the hypophosphataemia is free to stimulate renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
The resulting rise in 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption, producing hypercalciuria, a suppressed parathyroid hormone and a risk of stones and nephrocalcinosis.
This biochemical signature - a raised calcitriol with hypercalciuria - is the key discriminator from X-linked and other FGF23-mediated forms.
Treatment is with phosphate replacement alone; active vitamin D is not required and can aggravate the hypercalciuria.
Heterozygous relatives may show only hypercalciuria with stones or nephrocalcinosis, without overt bone disease.
Clinical features from childhood include bowing of the legs, bone pain, short stature, muscle weakness and dental problems.
reference.pathophysiology: NaPi-IIc, encoded by SLC34A3, is an apical sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter of the proximal tubule that, together with NaPi-IIa, reclaims filtered phosphate. Biallelic loss of NaPi-IIc function lowers the tubular maximum for phosphate reabsorption, so phosphate escapes into the urine and the serum phosphate falls, impairing mineralisation of growing bone and producing rickets and osteomalacia. Crucially, the disorder does not involve an excess of fibroblast growth factor 23; because FGF23 is low or normal, the hypophosphataemia is able to stimulate renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase and raise 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. This active vitamin D augments intestinal absorption of both phosphate and calcium, and the additional calcium load, in the face of an appropriately suppressed parathyroid hormone, is excreted in the urine as hypercalciuria, predisposing to nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis. This intact-to-elevated calcitriol axis fundamentally separates the condition from the FGF23-excess phosphopenic rickets and dictates that phosphate, rather than active vitamin D, is the appropriate replacement.
additionalDifferentials: X-linked hypophosphataemia (PHEX) and other FGF23-mediated forms with inappropriately normal or low calcitriol
Autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets (FGF23) and autosomal recessive forms (DMP1, ENPP1)
Tumour-induced osteomalacia from FGF23-secreting mesenchymal tumours
Fanconi syndrome and Dent disease, where phosphate wasting is part of a wider proximal leak
Nutritional vitamin D deficiency or calcium-deficiency rickets
Hypophosphatasia (ALPL), with a low alkaline phosphatase and raised substrate
Idiopathic hypercalciuria and other causes of paediatric nephrolithiasis
additionalInvestigations: Serum phosphate with the tubular maximum for phosphate corrected for filtration to confirm renal wasting
Fibroblast growth factor 23, which is low or normal and separates the disorder from FGF23-excess rickets
Parathyroid hormone, typically suppressed, together with serum calcium
Quantified urinary calcium and renal tract ultrasound for calculi or nephrocalcinosis
Skeletal radiographs and alkaline phosphatase to characterise the rickets
Molecular testing of SLC34A3, with screening of relatives for hypercalciuria
redFlags: Progressive limb deformity, bone pain or growth failure indicating active rickets
Nephrocalcinosis or recurrent calcium calculi from sustained hypercalciuria
Worsening hypercalciuria after inappropriate active vitamin D therapy
Fractures or severe osteomalacia in an affected adult
Features of a wider proximal tubulopathy suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Phosphate replacement heals the rickets and improves growth and symptoms in most patients, and the long-term outlook is generally good. Ongoing hypercalciuria and the associated risk of stones or nephrocalcinosis nonetheless require lifelong monitoring.
pitfalls: Giving active vitamin D as though this were X-linked hypophosphataemia - endogenous calcitriol is already high, and supplementation aggravates hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis.
Missing the diagnosis by not measuring 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and fibroblast growth factor 23, the parameters that distinguish it from FGF23-mediated rickets.
Overlooking heterozygous relatives who present only with hypercalciuria or stones.
Interpreting a suppressed parathyroid hormone as reassuring rather than as part of the expected pattern.
Confusing the isolated phosphate wasting with generalised Fanconi syndrome by failing to check other proximal solutes.
